📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pioner, a survival-shooter we said looked like "Stalker and Tarkov's alien baby" when we first laid eyes on it in 2021, is ending development and closing down. In an announcement posted today on Steam, developer GFAGames said further work on the game and continued operation of its servers requires more money, and it just doesn't have any.

"Over the past few months, we have been in talks with existing and potential partners about investment and new ways of working together that would allow us to preserve the project and the team," the studio wrote.

"We were unable to agree on the funding needed to continue the project. The studio no longer has sufficient funds of its own to continue development and keep the servers running.".

Pioner looked promising when it turned up at the PC Gaming Show in 2021: A mash-up of Stalker, Metro, and Escape From Tarkov that featured both a singleplayer campaign and online co-op and PvP survival action, all of it built around late Soviet-era technology.

It introduced into early access in December 2025 and worked its way to a peak concurrent player count of 1,686 on Steam a few months later—not huge, but far from catastrophic, and trending in the right direction.

In a recent development, those numbers tailed off badly over the summer, though, as the dev team struggled with technical issues and updates came at a much slower pace than promised. August saw player counts collapse almost completely, and by mid-September only a couple dozen people were still playing.

Industry observers note that numerous replies to the shutdown announcement call for refunds to be issued, but GFAGames hasn't commented on those demands at this point. It also hasn't noted when the game will actually be taken offline—I've reached out to ask and will enhancement if I receive a reply.

#4625. Amid soaring PC hardware prices, gaming monitors are getting cheaper and cheaper. Here's why, and what to buy

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2101 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Amid soaring PC hardware prices, gaming monitors are getting cheaper and cheaper. Here's why, and what to buy

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, hello, good local-time-zone-adjusted afternoon, and let's just say it's been a while.
  • Industry observers note that instead I speak of screens, where there is actually some very good news.
  • Also bear in mind we've had a fair old bit of inflation in recent years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hello, good local-time-zone-adjusted afternoon, and let's just say it's been a while. But I come back to you now at the turn of the technological tide. Well, sort of. Sadly I'm not here to predict an end to the ridiculous AI-fuelled chip crisis. That whole mess has a couple of years to run, surely.

Industry observers note that instead I speak of screens, where there is actually some very good news. In short, have you seen how cheap PC gaming monitors are? I mean remarkably, almost stupendously, cheap. I'm talking £60 / $60 for an entry-level 1080p panel with triple-digit refresh rate, sub-£200 / $250 for high-refresh 4K gaming. Heck, even OLED monitors now start with a "2" in both currencies.

Also bear in mind we've had a fair old bit of inflation in recent years. A 4K panel bought today for £200 is equivalent to paying roughly £150 back in 2020. All the while, that same £200 / $200 right now won't buy you a current-model gaming graphics card at all, even the most feeble example, and will barely secure a basic dual-channel 16GB DDR5 memory kit. Youch.

So, I think we can all agree monitors are cheap in the current chip-catastrophe context. The immediate question is why? The answer isn't all that complicated, actually. Most obviously, the display market isn't being devoured by the AI craze. All those data centres are stuffed with GPUs, memory chips and NAND flash, not monitors.

It has been revealed that by way of example, one of the largest fresh AI data centres on Earth is Microsoft's new Fairwater site in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin. It's thought to pack hundreds of thousands of Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. The cost doesn't bear thinking about, but those GPUs are built into what's known as "headless" server racks. In other words, they have no screens at all. Ultimately, the key compute hardware is all managed remotely, in which capacity the Fairwater facility is reported to at the moment have around 375 employees. If we generously assume each has two PC monitors, that's only 750 for the entire site.

AI isn't really driving demand on the end-user side of the equation, either. Put it this way: you don't need to buy a new phone, laptop or PC to access the latest models. At the same time, the display market is suffering from something of a glut of overcapacity. Chinese companies built out huge capacity in LCD panel manufacturing over the past decade, to the extent factories are now running underutilised. Meanwhile, even the OLED market is arguably oversupplied.

Sources indicate that in fact, Samsung and LG, the two significant noises in large OLED panel manufacturing (as opposed to OLED displays for tablets and phones), have been shifting emphasis away from TV panels to PC monitors because the latter offer better margins. Meanwhile, the AI boom has almost definitely meant lower demand for latest PCs. Certainly, the big research houses point to cratering PC sales thanks to higher component costs. Long story short, that's oodles of capacity combined with weakening demand. Like I noted, the explanation for cheap monitors isn't exactly rocket surgery, if you know what I mean.

According to recent reports, what is a bit more complicated is making sense of what's available today in the gaming monitor market. With so much choice, where exactly is the very best value to be found? And are there any remaining pain points?

Sources indicate that monitor specifications, to be sure, can be tricksy at the best of times. But if you're looking for some blanket rules to fling casually over the whole LCD monitor market - I'll be digging deeper into OLED tech another day - try these for size. Look for, at minimum, 300 nits brightness and 1ms response times. Refresh rates are a slightly more complicated call, but for the vast majority of games, 144Hz is plenty. For "esports-grade multiplayer fare like Counter-Strike or Dota 2, or I think a refresh in the high 200s will get the job done for most. If you'll benefit from more than that, you almost certainly know who you are already.

In a recent development, oh, and heavily favour IPS over VA panels. Exceptions exist: there are some decent "Rapid VA" panels these days and Samsung, in particular, does some nippy VA models. But a lot of the cheaper stuff is pretty slow and smeary, making VA a risky buy. Finally, don't worry too much about claimed HDR capability, save for the fact that HDR 400 certification at least means the monitor can do 400 nits. Unless a monitor has local dimming, it won't be truly HDR capable.

Anywho, one immediate and rather ironic matter is the growing mismatch between monitors and GPUs. For sure, it's great you can grab a high-refresh 4K monitor for such little money. It's almost hard to believe that you can have this 27-inch IPS MSI for sub-£200 (you're looking at $250 for the same model in the US), and it even has a 288Hz 1080p dual mode.

Industry observers note that I actually favour 32 inches with my 4K gaming, and that's naturally a little pricier, especially if you insist on an IPS - which again, you probably should. But even $350 for that kind of panel (here's a comparable model for £340 in the UK) is a fraction of what you'd have paid for a similarly specced model a few years ago. And it probably wouldn't have included dual-mode functionality.

Sources indicate that here's the problem, though. How are you going to drive the thing, what with its eight million-plus pixels? After all, the cheapest RTX 5090 on Newegg right now is over $6,500. So high-end Nvidia GPUs now cost about as much as a decent used car.

Industry observers note that of course, you might be surprised just how effective the likes of an AMD RX 9070 XT or Nvidia RTX 5070-class GPU is at 4K thanks to upscaling technologies including DLSS and FSR. The latest transformer model upscalers really do knock out pretty stellar image quality. Add in a bit of frame gen and you have a compelling combination of visual sharpness, reasonably low latency and nice smoothframe rates, even in the most demanding of games. Perhaps the one thing you can't do is enable full path tracing in a game like Cyberpunk 2077 and still expect a slick experience, but standard ray tracing remains an option.

The bigger snag, unsurprisingly, is that you can no longer bag a 5070 at (let alone below) its original £539 / $549 MSRP. Instead, you're looking at the thick end of £800 / $900. That's a bit of an ask for pairing with a £200 monitor, isn't it?

It has been revealed that I'd therefore argue that, for pure gaming purposes, the bang-for-buck sweet spot remains just where it's been sat twiddling its thumbs for the better part of a decade, namely 1440p. That applies to both its vanilla 16:9 aspect variety and my personally preferred ultrawide format, the latter being so very immersive and also pretty nifty for daily multi-tasking. Indeed, the 27-inch 1440p segment even brings the vibrant colours and infinite contrast of OLED panels into a reasonably affordable window.

In a recent development, by way of example, £179 (or $150) is enough for a circa 200Hz, IPS 1440p panel with super low (by IPS standards) pixel response, even if the 250-nit brightness is lower than I'd like. Meanwhile, as I write these words, pricing for significant-brand 27-inch 1440p gaming OLEDs kicks off at about £290 in the UK and roughly $270 in the US. Admittedly, those entry-level OLEDs come with some compromises, which I'll cover in a forthcoming post. But what you might call 'proper' OLED panels can be had around the low £300 / $300 mark - not throw-away money, for sure, but relatively accessible.

In a recent development, the 34-inch 1440p ultrawide segment is a bit trickier, however. The good news is that conventional LCD models can be had for relative peanuts, with prices starting at about £220 or $249 for game-focused, high-refresh models. But those two example both use a VA panel, which usually means inferior pixel response.

It has been revealed that IPS models are a little thin on the ground when it comes to 34-inch ultrawide, but sneaking in below £300 / $300 is generally possible. The real bummer is OLED, where going ultrawide invokes a massive premium. The best price I can find on a big-brand 34-inch ultrawide today is $629 for this Asus model in the US and £648 for this MSI option in the UK.

That's awfully toppy, especially when you consider that you can grab a 49-inch, 5,120x1,440 ultrawide OLED for barely any more money. I do actually quite like those 49-inch ultrawides, but I have to concede the ergonomics are challenging. However, 4K OLEDs in 27-inch and 32-inch formats can also be had for as much as £100 / $100 less than the current cheapest 34-inch 1440p ultrawides, which doesn't make much sense to me.

Again, with 4K, there's the challenge of keeping all those pixels updated. If you already have a sufficiently mighty graphics card, though, I a 32-inch 4K OLED can make a fantastic all-round option, and something like this MSI model for £549 would be absolutely lovely. You get good pixel density and lots of space for daily desktopping, plus OLED visuals and a large enough panel to be really get you into your games.

It's just a pity that 34-inch OLED ultrawides remain so weirdly expensive, it being a format that ticks so many different boxes. As for my own personal money-no-object pick, well, I'm typing these words on the upcoming Alienware AW3926QW, the 39-inch 5K2K beast with a Tandem WOLED panel and RGB subpixels.

Sources indicate that one could argue it's a relative steal at £1,079 or $1,100. I mean, it's pretty much peak current PC gaming display technology, and it's about half the price of what Nvidia's second-tier RTX 5080 graphics card is going for lately. Assuming you can even find one in stock.

At this point, the one major category I haven't covered is LCD monitors with mini-LED full-array local dimming. Cards on the table, I'm not a huge fan of mini-LED monitors. The detailed reasons for that are, perhaps, the subject for another day. But I've reviewed countless models and have yet to see one that didn't come with pretty serious compromises.

That mentioned, the technology has gotten a lot more accessible in the last 12 to 18 months, to the extent that 27-inch 1440p models start at just over $250. I've had that specific model in and came away pretty impressed. It's very, very punchy, and even factoring in the limitations of mini-LED versus OLED when it comes to lighting control and speed, I cannot deny the temptation.

Just for completeness, one further exception to the general rule of cheap gaming monitors involves ultra-high refresh monitors aimed at serious esports aficionados. I'm talking about panels like this 1,000Hz LG I sampled elsewhere. At £800 / $1,000 for a 25-inch 1080p IPS panel it's inevitably a niche proposition, and poor value by normal standards.

Sources indicate that I think a much better compromise for just about everyone, short of an actual esports pro, is to grab a larger, higher resolution monitor that offers one of those windowed 1080p modes running at about 500Hz or thereabouts. That way you've got a nice high-res panel for both work and play, as well as that ultra-low latency mode for when you want to dance around Dust 2 doling out the headshots or whatever.

Incidentally, I realise I've gone in a bit hot and heavy with the OLED content here, the implicit assumption being OLED is all that, and notably without addressing the obvious objections like the risk of burn-in. But all that, I hope you'll be pleased to hear, is very much the subject for my next RPS post on all things OLED.

Until then, all I can say is thank goodness PC monitors provide relative respite from the parlous state of much of the rest of the PC component market. It's absolutely brutal out there if you're building a gaming PC, but at least you'll get a lot of screen for your money.

Just to round things out, if anyone has any specific queries at any given price point, form factor or panel type, shout out below and I'll try to steer you in the direction of a decent model.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that there are several ways players, notably Twitch streamers and content creators, have been able to do that over the years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Lobby shopping" is what Call of Duty: Warzone players have been calling the ability to check the skill level of players in a lobby prior to joining it, enabling them to pass on those that include a lot of tough competition.

It has been revealed that there are several ways players, notably Twitch streamers and content creators, have been able to do that over the years. But the use of one app in particular - Warzone Agent - has been considered by many to be cheating, and Activision is finally doing something about it.

Alongside the launch of Modern Warfare 4's version of Warzone and the game's first season of post-launch content, Call of Duty's anti-cheat team Ricochet has revealed it's officially cracking down on Warzone Agent.

"Yesterday, we began taking action against Warzone Agent, a paid, unauthorised third party tool that lets users lobby shop in Warzone," the developer revealed in a post on X. "Ricochet anti-cheat will block players attempting to load the software and instruct them to unload it before accessing multiplayer.".

Having the ability to cherrypick the lobby with the lowest-skilled players possible bypasses the game's matchmaking algorithm, potentially ruining the game for the dozens of other players in the match. Historically, content creators have used the app (and other methods) to post impressive kill records.

Recent findings suggest that "Boosting services flood lobbies with low effort accounts used to farm XP and complete challenges. Those accounts can later be sold as Ranked Play ready, directly feeding the cheating marketplace.".

More than 20,000 boosting-related accounts have been removed since the launch of Modern Warfare 4, according to the developer, and Ricochet will "continue to apply pressure" in this area.

The quality of multiplayer was a particular highlight in Eurogamer's review of Modern Warfare 4, in which Dom Peppiatt lauded the complexity of weapon handling, which works without taking away from accessibility of the gunplay.

Meanwhile, the cultural impact of GTA 6's imminent arrival continues with a takeover of swanky department store Selfridges in London, which has a custom Ferrari parked in a window and an extensive range of expensive merch to buy.

It's not all good news for Rockstar, though. The company is also fighting an employment tribunal in Scotland relating to the sudden firing of 31 staff from Rockstar North this time last year. Rockstar alleges this was done for gross misconduct reasons, whereas the fired staff maintain it was done in the name of union busting. The results of that hearing are expected close to GTA 6's release, on 19th November.

It will be available for PC via Steam. A release date was not announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page:.

Super Meat Boy is a tough as nails platformer originally released to much fanfare and great acclaim in 2010. It is held as a gold standard in difficult but fair platforming. You play as Meat Boy, a boy with no skin who leaves blood everywhere, who is saving his girlfriend, Bandage Girl, from Dr. Fetus, a fetus in a jar wearing a top hat and a monocle.

Super Meat Boy Again+ everything you remember from Super Meat Boy presented through the wonderful lens of nostalgia with stuff added to it. Everything is upcoming but familiar. We have new art, new music, new cutscenes, new secrets, and new stuff.

Since 2010, millions of people played Super Meat Boy, all the secrets are known, all the levels are mastered, all the characters unlocked, so we have to give fans familiar with the game something to pull their hair out over. That’s the “+” in Again+, and no, we won’t spoil it. You’ll go into it blind like you did the first time you played Super Meat Boy.

For our old fans, we want to present the game as you remember it through the wonderful lens of nostalgia.

For our new fans, we want to give you a great looking, easy to pick up but difficult to master platformer that you may have missed because it came out like four years after YouTube was invented.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, earlier this year, Pearl Abyss apologized for the presence of AI-generated art in Crimson Desert—not because it had used generative AI, mind, but because players saw it. And it seems like the odds we might see more of it in the future are going up, as the studio said in its Q3 2026 earnings letter (via Eurogamer) that it will be going even deeper on AI-powered development in the future.

According to recent reports, the first reference to AI comes midway through the letter: "While we previously validated game systems only after implementing them manually, we now utilize AI to rapidly validate diverse design concepts prior to actual implementation," it states. "This enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed.".

The studio immediately clarified, though, that AI "serves strictly as a tool to support concept validation and pipeline productivity," and that gameplay and content development "remain fully driven by our development team.".

Sources indicate that the future will see more of the same, with the same caveats. "We are integrating AI technologies to enhance development productivity and overall quality," Pearl Abyss writes. "AI is being utilized across various stages of development—including the automation of repetitive tasks, content creation support, and test optimization—and we are expanding its implementation throughout our entire development pipeline.

Sources indicate that "We view AI not as a substitute for human developers, but as a tool to elevate development efficiency and quality. We will continue to expand our application of AI to deliver higher-fidelity games to the market more expeditiously.".

That essentially repeats what Pearl Abyss said in February when players discovered the presence of generative AI art in Crimson Desert: It acknowledged that "some 2D visual props" had been created by AI during the early stages of development, but said they were supposed to be replaced "following final work and review by our art and development teams, with work that aligned with our quality standards and creative direction.".

Industry observers note that the studio also admitted that it had not "clearly disclosed our use of AI" in the development process, and promised to be more transparent about it in the future. This letter certainly could be seen as a step in that direction.

If you don't need quite as much coverage, smaller configurations, including a single satellite node, is also discounted as part of Amazon's early Black Friday sale. The system uses tri-band Wi-Fi 7 technology to spread your connection across three bands, with combined speeds of up to 11,000Mbps. It also supports wider 320MHz channels, though you'll need compatible Wi-Fi 7 devices to take advantage of those faster connections. If you prefer wired connections for devices that need a more stable link, the main router has three 2.5GbE LAN ports and a 2.5GbE WAN port, while the satellite offers two 2.5GbE LAN ports. This gives you plenty of room to connect a gaming console, desktop PC, or smart TV, and you can also use wired backhaul if your home has Ethernet cabling.

Recent findings suggest that once everything is connected, you can handle setup and day-to-day management through Netgear's Orbi app, while a web dashboard offers additional settings (for anyone who wants more control over their network), including VPN access and port forwarding, notes this PCMag review. There's no USB connectivity or 10GbE support, and some of its more advanced security and parental control features require a separate subscription after a free 30-day trial. Its Smart Parental Controls, for instance, cost $7.99 per month or $69.99 annually.

My firstest-ever Golden Joystick Awards, which took place last night in London, was marred somewhat by 1) a gin & tonic costing eleven quid and 2) my view of the stage being directly obscured by its own rigging. Nonetheless, I did crane enough to get a good view at the reveal of The Sound of Fury, a musically-minded hack 'n' slash in which a troubled classical musician descends into Hell to save a friend from the Devil.

Industry observers note that it's not out until late 2027, and the strength of its monster-battering will of course lay in how it feels in the hand. I like the look of this one, though. While it doesn't appear to be a full-on rhythm action game in the Hi-Fi Rush or Dead as Disco vein, it's clearly trying incorporate our glum hero's virtuosity with both visual and thematic flair: spinning attacks are accentuated by trails of sheet music staves, and at least one move inflicts enemies with uncontrollable bouts of dancing. Weapons also take the form of instruments, the trailer being particularly keen to show grand pianos being powerbombed into demon heads. "You dropped your... keys," I will say, to the demons. Heh heh heh.

In a recent development, also of note is The Sound of Fury's unusual interpretation of Hell, which rather than the usual Biblical/Nordic/Ancient Greek depictions we get in games, is a washed-out mashup of what the Steam page calls "humanity's darkest chapters." Thus, you fight not red-skinned horned imps but gasmasked soldiers and Klu Klux Klansmen, with history-spanning anomalies distorting an otherwise 19th century-flavoured fantasyscape. The laws of time evidently aren't followed here, not least when the protag whips out a Flying V guitar to give the Grim Reaper a different kind of axe wound.

It has been revealed that I can't find much else out about developers and self-publishers Games By Wojtek, with that pluralisation assuming 'they' aren't just one person named Wojtek, but The Sound of Fury looks to be his/their debut game. Hopefully it gets a demo, in due course, so we can try tickling its ivories ourselves.

Nvidia's board of directors has launched an investigation into its own CEO Jensen Huang, after a report by the Upcoming York Times claimed he had been participating in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to having an affair in a manufacturer-wide statement, apologising to his wife as well as to Nvidia employees. Following this acknowledgement, independent investigators are looking into whether or not he's been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort".

According to recent reports, per the New York Times article, the alleged spy was named as Megaspeed executive and Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang or Huang Le. Jensen Huang wrote in his internal letter: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.".

Industry observers note that with regard to security concerns surrounding the CEO of US-based company Nvidia potentially sharing information with a spy, Huang confirmed that the Nvidia board of directors had initiated an investigation. He added: "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully." The Nvidia board has remarked it has "no reason to believe either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.".

In a recent development, huang will remain CEO of Nvidia while the investigation is conducted. The Upcoming York Times report also claimed that US government officials did not believe Huang knew of Alice Huang's alleged intelligence activities for China.

Following the internal letter from Jensen Huang, Nvidia stock took a tumble from $162bn to $150bn. Nvidia, a juggernaut in the video game hardware industry, is also a key player in the global generative AI industry, which is at the moment carrying the US economy as other sectors struggle. The firm is responsible for AI technology like DLSS 5, which generates lighting, shadows and more using generative AI.

Concerns around the Chinese AI sector passing the American industry has been a core argument against AI development slowdown or regulation, and it's also why Huang's affair may be a matter of national interest.

It has been revealed that if you're a CK3 player—and you should be; it's number eight on our Top 100 list for a reason—then Paradox's next expansion should be on your radar. While everyone else is focused on Grand Theft Auto, you could be engaging in the grandest theft of all: Commerce.

Silk and Silver is all about mercantilism: Merchant families can jockey for trade route monopolies and use their wealth to lobby for influence, while new Republic governments offer patrician dynasties a venue to vie for dominance in the constitutional Assembly—potentially forming commercial or military pacts with other Republics. It's also got a lot of Italian content in it. Everyone loves Italian content.

Crusader Kings 3: Silk and Silver introduces on November 17.

Among the cozier offerings arriving on Steam during GTA 6 week, Spirit Crossing is a building, crafting, and decorating MMO set in a world seemingly populated entirely by art students and befriendable spirits.

Borrowing a page from Sky: Children of the Light, it's only as much of an MMO as you want it to be: other players are only fully visible in your world if you mutually choose to engage with one another. Otherwise, you're free to roam its pastel soulscape and build out your own little corner of paradise solo for as long as you prefer.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Spirit Crossing introduces on November 16.

Listen. I know. It's 2026. I feel the same suspicions that you do when you see a game with full-on pixel illustrations like this on Steam nowadays. But the developers of Harma insist that it's "developed entirely by human creators and does not contain any contents or assets generated by AI tools." Which is good, because it looks neat, and I want to believe.

Sources indicate that it's a roguelike deckbuilder that has both a story-driven campaign and a replayable "Dimensional Rift" mode, which should provide plenty of opportunity to continue admiring the work of its pixel artists. Assuming there were, in fact, pixel artists. They wouldn't lie to me, right? Please?

Harma launches in early access on November 16.

It has been revealed that melvor Idle is for one of the most particular types of guys, and whether or not you're one of them should be clarified as soon as I say this sentence: Melvor Idle 2 is like Old School RuneScape with all the parts that aren't a skill grind stripped away. It's 100% gathering items so you can get better at gathering items so you can gather better items. It's pure, uncut clicking and waiting as numbers go up.

According to recent reports, it's so thoroughly for RuneScape guys that, after the success of the first Melvor Idle, Jagex brought the operation under its publishing wing. If that's for you, I'm not judging. In many ways, you're living a more honest life than I am.

Melvor Idle 2 rolls out in early access on November 17.

If you do not yet acknowledge the awesome power of the roundabout, it is time to learn. Trafficity is a game about traffic. There are cars, and they must go places. But only so many cars can go to one place at once.

This is the crux on which our world is both built and broken.

According to recent reports, and now it is yours to solve—using a toolkit of gridless road design tools, fully-customizable traffic lights, and dynamic interchange simulation. Somewhere, in another game, your uncouth lessers are disrupting this great task with the stealing and crashing of your vehicular charges. But now, you answer to a higher calling. The traffic must flow.

Trafficity debuts on November 16.

Publisher Devolver Digital is taking Grand Theft Auto 6 on directly with this fake remake (re-fake?) of an "unreleased" platformer starring its bizarre mascot, Volvy. Titled Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed, the game challenges players to traverse four zany platforming worlds, using Volvy's grotesquely swollen hand to smash enemies, punch through blocks, and fist-i-copter across gaps.

Sources indicate that while Volvy's Adventure boils down to a playable joke, it is a pretty stylish one. Developer doinksoft has clearly put a lot of care into the game's crisp retro pixel art, while the platforming seems to have a decent amount of physicality to it. The game will release on the same day as Grand Theft Auto six at a discounted price, so it'll be interesting to see whether it can cut through the noise of Vice City's hyper-real traffic.

Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed debuts on November 19.

Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (410 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking.
  • Industry observers note that as reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device.
  • In a recent development, there are two silver linings here, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always vital to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

Industry observers note that as reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

In a recent development, there are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for customers to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to problem these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

According to recent reports, this flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

It has been revealed that to see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this concern. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For example, the magazine kicks off with a statement from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, who discusses the past 25 years of the brand and where it's going in the future - similar to a statement she shared on social media recently.
  • This time though, she talks less about how games will be made, and more about the fact that she wants to take "creative risks" while also acknowledging that her team won't "get every decision right" along the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday, we talked about the Project Helix part of the Xbox 25th anniversary magazine that's been made available to read in full on the official Xbox Wire website, and there's plenty more interesting stuff where that came from!

For example, the magazine kicks off with a statement from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, who discusses the past 25 years of the brand and where it's going in the future - similar to a statement she shared on social media recently.

This time though, she talks less about how games will be made, and more about the fact that she wants to take "creative risks" while also acknowledging that her team won't "get every decision right" along the way.

Here are the key parts of the statement:.

Industry observers note that "There are plenty of milestones from the past 25 years, and you'll find many of them in these pages. But I don't think the story of Xbox is really a story about any given hardware, launch or number. It is a story about people. Players turned games into friendships, rivalries and family traditions. They played with roommates who became lifelong friends, with brothers and sisters who moved across the country, with parents who got older and kids who eventually picked up the controller themselves. Some of the people we played with 25 years ago are no longer here. Some are sitting next to us, now playing with a new generation.".

Recent findings suggest that "We should be proud of that history. But we shouldn't be trapped by it.".

Recent findings suggest that "Games are alive. The best ones find latest players and new creators. They move between generations. They get changed, remade and occasionally broken apart and rebuilt into something nobody expected. Twenty-five years in, Xbox should have that same restlessness.".

Recent findings suggest that "We have been given the chance to care for some of the most loved games and characters in the world. Our job is to protect what makes them special without protecting them from change. To keep making newly introduced things. To take creative risks. To meet players wherever they choose to play. And to make sure someone discovering Xbox for the first time today can feel the same possibility that someone felt turning on that first console in 2001.".

Recent findings suggest that "We don't get every decision right. No company that is still making things does. But we can keep listening, learning and building. Twenty-five years ago, a relatively small group of people imagined that Microsoft could make a game console. It was an improbable idea. They made it real. I like that as our inheritance.".

In a recent development, there's definitely some interesting stuff in here, including Sharma's insistence that Xbox shouldn't be "trapped" by its past, that her team should be willing to experiment and take risks in the future, and an admission that not every decision will work out for the best. That's pretty refreshing to hear, and it certainly reads well on paper at least.

Let's see what happens, eh? Xbox's 25th anniversary has been a weird year, full of ups and downs, but it seems like there's a cautious optimism circulating around the fanbase regarding things like console updates, exclusives and various other initiatives that have been introduced since the Xbox CEO took the helm at the start of the year.

These next 25 years are going to be fascinating to say the least!

What are your thoughts on this latest statement from Asha Sharma? Tell us down in the comments below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that don't say that Sony can't time a discount well - the brand has finally given its DualSense Edge pro controller an early Black Friday deal, the week of GTA 6's release. I've seen previous Black Fridays, Prime Days, and other huge AAA releases happen, and the price of the DualSense Edge hasn't budged, but as soon as it's being considered one of the best controllers for GTA 6, the discounts finally arrive.

In a recent development, if you're a Prime member and you order this today, there's a good chance it'll arrive with you before the 19th, when the game becomes available to play. It's a whole $30 off the cost of the gamepad, which brings the $200 price tag to a much more palatable $169 at Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that the discount stands for both the Black and White models of the DualSense Edge, and the price is the same at Walmart if you want to try your luck at collecting it at a nearby store before the 19th. In the UK, the price has come down to £149.99.

$169 at Walmart UK: £149.99 at Amazon.

According to recent reports, the last time we saw the DualSense Edge drop to this price was back in June, but its lowest price ever is $159.99, only $10 more affordable than it is now. According to the Amazon price history data I'm seeing, it's dropped as low as it is currently only three or four times since its arrival on the shelves in 2023. Before May last year, it had only dipped its toe in the discount aisle down to $200 or even $195 - which were sorry excuses for discounts.

In a recent development, personally, seeing as Rockstar won't launch GTA 6 on PC at the same time as consoles, the DualSense Edge is the controller I'd recommend experiencing the game with if you have the budget. I noted a similar thing last week when I recommended other gamepads for GTA 6, but seeing as Rockstar has been in cahoots with PlayStation for launch, there are all sorts of DualSense perks you can enjoy in the game. The DualSense Edge will get access to all of those PlayStation-bespoke features, but give you more comfort and functionality than the stock controller (which is also discounted at the moment, FYI).

Recent findings suggest that what are you actually getting? Besides the hold-all charging case the Edge comes in, you also get some swappable thumbsticks, two magnetic back paddles (that come in various shapes), and refined, rounded corners to the bottoms of the grips. These make a genuine difference to how comfortable the DualSense is in your hands, and trigger stop switches give you the chance to find the squeeze that feels best for you.

It has been revealed that there's more you can do with the DualSense on the software side, and clever profile-switching buttons rest below the thumbsticks. In a practical sense, I think most players will set these up and not touch them often, so the paragraph above lists the stuff you'll actually care about when playing GTA.

According to recent reports, what you're not getting here is any sort of enhanced battery life - so don't expect that to be any less dire than the regular DualSense. Similarly, the Edge still uses potentiometer thumbstick modules, which means they're just as prone to stick drift from prolonged use. That's a real shame, but at least you'll have access to haptic feedback and adaptive trigger resistance, which the other best PS5 candidates don't have due to licensing challenges.

Industry observers note that owlcat Games has revealed a release date for its tactical role-playing sequel Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy. The game arrives 28th January, 2027 on PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S/X. A Switch 2 release date will be provided "at a later date", a press release claims.

In a recent development, warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy follows the good work laid down by Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader a couple of years ago. "Rogue Trader nails the 40k setting and provides an appropriately massive narrative filled with meaty tactical combat, though some bugs and poor performance hold it back," wrote Caeyln Ellis in Eurogamer's Warhammer 40,000 Rogue Trade review.

It has been revealed that dark Heresy changes things by casting you as an Inquisitor and tasking you with hunting down heretics and purging the world of dark influences, as one is wont to do in the 41st century, it seems. And developer Owlcat has apparently overhauled many of the systems underpinning the adventure.

Sources indicate that there's a beta that's been running for a while that offers a complete first Act to try, and it's accessible if you buy a Founders edition of the game. This beta, incidentally, disappears 7th January, when Owlcat prepares the game for launch.

Meanwhile, Owlcat is making a substantially different RPG based around the popular Expanse license - a game that's much more closely inspired by Mass Effect. That project recently recruited the help of former Dragon Age writer David Gaider, and it will no doubt hope to fill a much-lamented hole created recently by the cancellation of Mass Effect 5.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since we're already sharing trailers from non-Geoff awards shows, here's another: a first in-motion look at Lola's Familiars: Prison of Argnoh, a 2D side-scroller and "lite-vania" that sees its shy witch-in-training making her first summonable friends. Then, borrowing their powers to bust out of a dark fantasy oubliette.

Recent findings suggest that it looks like this'll be a mix of passively familiar-enhanced punching and more active, mayhaps traditionally Metroid-y power upgrades, Lola's ghastly pals looming over her tiny frame when called upon. It's all presented in a hand-drawn, lightly anime-ish style, complete with a story setup straight out of Saturday morning TV – Lola's only stuck in Skullcatraz because of a summoning-gone-wrong that occurred in pursuit of her school's unlikely Ofsted-compliant 'familiar contest'. I've attended school several times, and will attest that non-sporting contests, which students remain unaware of until seeing a poster for them, do not exist outside of childrens' television*.

This doesn't seem to be kid fodder, though. Lola's a bean but the familiars, and the prison's other denizens, are growling towers of jaws and decaying flesh. Developers Caracal Games are promising they'll star in a "heartfelt and emotionally resonant story about growth," to balance out the grimness, though I'm less clear on a following blurb point that declares it a "lite-vania," into which you'll "dive into exploration, trial-and-error and platforming, without feeling frustrated." While this might just be an attempt to assuage fears that this'll a Hollow Knight- or Nine Sols-style controller-thrower, I do wonder how one goes light on 'vania. Maybe some of the ability gates open if you just ask them nicely?

According to recent reports, that aside, I'm already quite charmed by Lola's Familiars, especially the designs of its bag-eyed wallflower of a heroine and her contrastingly hench minions. Release date is TBC, but the Steam page is up.

*Granted, no TV example was ever as egregiously misleading as Jack Black vehicle School of Rock, which convinced me - then a barely-pubescent aspiring bassist - that winning a local Battle of the Bands would pay out thousands in cash, as opposed to the drinks rounds and packs of guitar strings I'd end up competing for a few years later.

Conan: The Black Pyramid shoves the titular barbarian into a very Hades-inspired action roguelite with the addition of a few other familiar heroes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I feel like one thing I only sort of miss from my youth, viewed through the lenses of those rose tinted goggles, is the established intellectual property game that just copies the formula of another, successful game.
  • Conan: The Black Pyramid puts you in the hotseat as the titular barbarian, of course, but also as other characters from the series like Solomon Kane, Dark Agnes, and apparently, more!
  • Where it is similar to Hades lies in the fact that the titular triangle changes in form each time you go in it, and of course there are different abilities and buffs to pick up along the way to aid you in your quest.

It has been revealed that I feel like one thing I only sort of miss from my youth, viewed through the lenses of those rose tinted goggles, is the established intellectual property game that just copies the formula of another, successful game. Obviously there are plenty of genres that are trendy to imitate, but how often do you see something that's just sort of "thing you know slapped on top of game you know?" Perhaps that's a tad mean, but I do genuinely have a fondness for such games, so I'm quite pleased by the announcement of Conan: The Black Pyramid, an action roguelite RPG that so clearly went to Supergiant Games' School of Hades you have to admire the boldness just a little bit.

Conan: The Black Pyramid puts you in the hotseat as the titular barbarian, of course, but also as other characters from the series like Solomon Kane, Dark Agnes, and apparently, more! So, immediately, a notable enough difference from Hades, and one that seems like a neat take. As one of them you then "Descend into eldritch chambers of the Black Pyramid, a mysterious and dangerous place that defies the logic of space and time. Confront the shadows of the champions themselves and piece together the dark secrets of their past.".

Where it is similar to Hades lies in the fact that the titular triangle changes in form each time you go in it, and of course there are different abilities and buffs to pick up along the way to aid you in your quest. Each character has their own combination of weapons and abilities, so it does sound like you can mix it up quite nicely. There is, also, 2-player online co-op (sorry to the couch lovers, I suppose), adding to the ways it differs and making it a tad more friendly for those that have exactly one friend who also loves Conan.

According to recent reports, overall, seems like a fresh enough take on Hades while still trying to find some amount of its own identity. And hey, Hades is great, so I'm never upset about having a little bit more of that kind of game. No release date attached to Conan: The Black Pyramid just yet, but it is planned to arrive sometime in 2027. You can check it out on Steam here.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • "The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," the booklet reads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a year after its initial release, physical versions of Hollow Knight: Silksong are finally arriving on players' doorsteps. It's the same brilliant and sometimes thrillingly cruel Metroidvania Eurogamer gave five stars to, except this time a pack-in booklet seemingly reveals the existence of multiple "free content packs" alongside the Sea of Sorrow DLC.

Hollow Knight: Silksong's physical editions were originally set to be delivered from 10th November, but some early handovers have given us a peek inside the box. Redditor Me_975 posted pictures of their Nintendo Switch 2 Edition, and there's a few interesting tidbits tucked away - most notably in the manual's chapter on Content Packs.

"The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," the booklet reads. "Prepare for even more adventures filled with new friends, new abilities, and new ferocious foes!".

Recent findings suggest that developer Team Cherry confirmed aims for post-launch Silksong support last year, but remained pretty tight-lipped about what exactly that would look like. The indie outfit then announced the nautically themed Sea of Sorrow expansion, though we now have proper confirmation there's more content packs still to come, which shouldn't be a huge shocker considering all the free post-launch love Hollow Knight (the first one) received.

Speaking of Sea of Sorrow, that's mentioned here too: "In the first giant expansion, voyage across and beneath a salt-stricken ocean brimming with mystery and menace.".

Sea of Sorrow's original release window was a vague 2026 - time's a-ticking, Team Cherry. Still no release date so far, but the booklet does say it's "Coming Soon." Of course, Team Cherry are quite infamous for working on games until they balloon wildly out of control. After all, Silksong was once upon a time intended to be a Hollow Knight DLC, but with games this detailed, I can't really complain about waiting a little extra.

If you are interested in owning Silksong physically, it comes with a major map of Pharloom and the rest of the booklet also includes some really lovely art seemingly ripped straight from the game, as well.

Indiana Jones and the Great Circle once had a Grand Theft Auto-inspired wanted system, because MachineGames was 'afraid' players would kill all the Nazis 'with just guns'

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pcgamer

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Indiana Jones and The Great Circle offered such a great depiction of everyone's favourite Nazi-thumping archaeologist that it's hard to imagine developer MachineGames building that game any differently.
  • One of the hardest problems MachineGames struggled with was the presence of guns—specifically, how to stop players from just blasting through armies of Nazis without making guns less fun to use.
  • In a recent development, since MachineGames wanted The Great Circle to be true to Spielberg's films, they needed guns to be a part of Indy's toolset but not the default response to every problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Indiana Jones and The Great Circle offered such a great depiction of everyone's favourite Nazi-thumping archaeologist that it's hard to imagine developer MachineGames building that game any differently. Yet according to design director Jens Andersson, getting the Indy feel of The Great Circle right represented a significant challenge for the Swedish studio.

One of the hardest problems MachineGames struggled with was the presence of guns—specifically, how to stop players from just blasting through armies of Nazis without making guns less fun to use. Speaking to FRVR, Andersson explained that having satisfying firearms in The Great Circle was "non-negotiable" as "we have a lot of people at Machine[Games] that love guns".

In a recent development, since MachineGames wanted The Great Circle to be true to Spielberg's films, they needed guns to be a part of Indy's toolset but not the default response to every problem. One partial solution was to make reloading slow, encouraging players to use other tools like Indy's whip or his fists, but this alone wasn't enough.

"We had so many designs to try and get around that," Andersson continued. "For example, a GTA star level system when you shoot someone and reinforcements [start] coming in." The thinking here seems to have been to discourage players from going overboard with loud weapons. "Because we were so afraid that this would be the default thing that the player would do. They take down a guy, they see a gun on the floor, and they clear the whole area with just guns.".

Sources indicate that in the end, the solution MachineGames stumbled on was to provide alternative, breakable melee weapons ranging from frying pans to violins. These abundant, lightly comedic tools encouraged players to embrace the improvisational nature of how Indy fights, offering a quick knockout both in stealth and when the player's ammunition ran dry.

Remarkably, Andersson says that breakable weapons "got in very late" during development. But when the studio "saw how effective it was, that's when we started putting all this weird stuff in. The violin, all of this weird stuff that makes it a little slapstick-y, but not slapstick.".

This system proved instrumental in getting the final balance of Indy's combat right, where stealth and fisticuffs are the primary approach, while guns tend to be a last resort. "We penalised shooting so much in that game. I know a lot of people are frustrated about that, but many more people love it," Andersson claims. "The thing that really fixed it was that we made melee combat so interesting, fun, and easy. Not easy challenge-wise, but just it's easy to get into. You stealth up, you hit someone from behind, the breakable weapon system was super important to do that. 'Oh, there's a new weapon, it's a fly swatter, I want to try this.'".

Keep up to date with the most crucial stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Ultimately, Indy's dynamic combat was a big part of what made it Machine Games' best game to date, earning it a score of 86 in PC Gamer's Indiana Jones and the Great Circle Review. Whether we'll see another Indy game from Machine Games is still up in the air. But if it does happen, it probably won't be soon, as the studio has just confirmed that's it's working on Wolfenstein 3.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy newly introduced Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thursday is a significant day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially debuts on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy newly introduced Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays states the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into concerns. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent problems when Ocarina of Time introduces tomorrow.

  • He reveals as much in a upcoming short over on YouTube, asking, "What's the thing I regret the most at Valve?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Valve developer Chet Faliszek – writer behind the likes of Half-Life 2, Portal and its sequel, Team Fortress 2, Left 4 Dead, and even Counter-Strike: Global Offensive – has one big regret about his time at the Steam tech giant: a joke he didn't make.

Yes, you read that right. He reveals as much in a upcoming short over on YouTube, asking, "What's the thing I regret the most at Valve? I was there for 12 years. So, what's the thing that I regret, that I did or didn't do?" Apparently, after sitting on this question for some time, he's become brave enough to publicly share his answer – an answer he thinks of "almost every year," as it weighs that heavy in his mind. Brace yourselves for this recollection, y'all.

Industry observers note that "If you remember, Valve had Steam Dev Days. We actually had a really early Steam Dev Days where I spoke at, and I spoke horribly, and I made a note that I've got to learn how to speak in public. I'm still not good at it, but it was just so bad. I was just shaking. It was just horrible. So, at this point, when Steam Dev Days two comes around, I'm like, 'Hey, I'll help out.'" Valve then decided to make him the host.

It has been revealed that the joke Faliszek mustered up was "going to put Gabe on the spot" – a joke about his polo shirt, to be precise. "My joke was, 'And here's Gabe Newell modeling the latest in polo,' because he always wore a polo shirt. 'Today's selection is polo after dark.'" The dev knew Newell would "lean into it" had he mentioned it, but he kept it to himself and laughed "so hard" without ever, uh, actually making the joke out loud.

Apparently that's nothing fresh for him, as he's often "laughing at jokes I don't say out loud because I'm thinking, 'That's going to push it.'" He does, again, regret not making this one in particular, though. "I regret that. I should have said that joke. That was a good joke. I know it's not the greatest joke, but at the time with Gabe walking in his black polo, it would have worked." And, honestly, I'd have to agree.

To this day, I seldom ever see Newell not wearing a polo shirt… if ever. I hope he tunes into Faliszek's channel and hears the joke, however, even if it's a good few years after it should've been spoken out loud.

Epic Games' Tim Sweeney says Steam's AI disclosure is "unfair to developers who use AI to make good games" because it associates AI "with bad games.".

  • Those stats should bode well for the series' next romp God of War: Laufey - which sees Faye take the spotlight across a multi-mythological afterlife and was recently delayed into May 2027 - even if PlayStation moves away from PC ports for its signature single-player games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

God of War: Ragnarok is the generation's best-selling and highest-earning PlayStation Studios game, according to a new report, but the full top 10 list has a few nice surprises.

Industry observers note that in the four years since its PS5 release and two years since its PC port, God of War: Ragnarok has reportedly sold just over 20m copies and generated $1.4b in revenue, according to estimates from Alinea Analytics. About 27.5 percent of the 15m copies it sold on console came from physical editions, and the action blockbuster apparently sold a further 1.1m this year alone. Not bad, boy.

Those stats should bode well for the series' next romp God of War: Laufey - which sees Faye take the spotlight across a multi-mythological afterlife and was recently delayed into May 2027 - even if PlayStation moves away from PC ports for its signature single-player games.

Kratos and Atreus only narrowly beat out perhaps the biggest superhero of them all: Marvel's Spider-Man 2, a game that reportedly made a whopping $1.3b off 19.1m copies across PS5 and PC. The Spidey sequel should keep swinging even higher as the years chug on, though - the report states that sales always surge during the holiday months, and this year's significant screen behemoth Spider-Man: Brand New Day led to an even bigger spike than usual.

Racing sim royalty Gran Turismo 7 ($841m), bug-squashing phenomenon Helldivers 2 ($786m), robo-dino sequel Horizon: Forbidden West ($485m), vengeful spirit sim Ghost of Yotei ($410m), undead remake The Last of Us Part 1 ($341m), multidimensional romp Ratchet and Clank: Rift Apart ($334m), Stellar Blade ($316m) and delightful throwback Astro Bot ($292m) round out the top 10 games published by PlayStation Studios this generation.

It has been revealed that it's worth noting that Helldivers 2 and Stellar Blade were developed by studios outside the PlayStation umbrella, but the console maker still published both upon release. Ghost of Yotei's performance is also particularly impressive since Sucker Punch's sequel has only been out for a year and didn't get the benefit of a PC port, like many of its PS5 siblings. The success couldn't save Sucker Punch from recent layoffs, however.

On PlayStation's decision to kill disc-based physical releases, analyst Rhys Elliott noted that the bottom five games in the list together made $281.7m this year alone: "PlayStation wants those numbers to be bigger in the coming years, which is one of the reasons it's killing the disc (alongside the better margins it and publishers get through digital.)".

According to recent reports, look at you, you lucky devil, you're being treated to a new Warhammer 40,000: Darktide class next month! This class is called the Sisters Novitiate, a group of wonderfully violent women with a penchant for crossbows, burning people alive and putting a stop to anyone that dares to oppose the God-Emperor. Neato!

In a recent development, according to a blog post accompanying the reveal of the class, the Sisters Novitiate work a tad differently compared to other classes available in the game. "Unlike other classes, the Sisters Novitiate are able to choose from six divine and devastating Acts of Faith, as opposed to blitz and combat abilities," the post explains. "Their abilities draw upon reserves of Faith, allowing them to unleash brutal Neural Whip attacks to the inspiring Icon of Purity and protective prayers. Faith can take many forms for the Sisters Novitiate, each channeling the Emperor's divine will and bringing his wrath upon his enemies.".

You build up their Faith while fighting, in turn choosing from a selection of doctrines and pledges in their talent tree, "each shaping how Faith is both accumulated and put to use. Any two Acts of Faith can be equipped at a time, allowing players to choose how their Novitiate will unleash righteous fury on the battlefield." I mentioned crossbows, right? Well, I stand lore corrected, as what they technically have is the Condemnor Stakethrower, which "pins what remains of their enemies to the walls." They do also have access to a flamethrower, a big ole mace, your classic sword and shield, and whatever the hell a "Penitent Eviscerator.".

Recent findings suggest that this DLC class also comes the same day as a free update, which will introduce the Metlagun, equipable by the Sisters Novitiate as well as the Veteran. Apparently there'll be more information on the free update soon. Oh, and the release date! It's December 7th, so a little under a month away. I'm sure you can (Dark)tide over the next few weeks by rewatching the gnarly reveal trailer.

  • Industry observers note that the upgrade isn't available yet, but will be coming to the game in early 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Star Wars Galactic Racer is my favourite game of the year so far. It's an incredible racing title that even surpasses the original Star Wars Episode 1 Racer in my view, and I've had so much fun with the campaign and online multiplayer.

There's just one downside that everyone's been pointing out since it was revealed, and that's the absence of local split-screen multiplayer. With that in mind, the development team have found a way to implement it in a fresh enhancement.

Industry observers note that the upgrade isn't available yet, but will be coming to the game in early 2027. Alongside it will be a upcoming mode called Free Play, which is where you'll be able to freely choose your vehicle, character, planet and race track.

"We’ve heard you! Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to bring a brand latest mode, Free Play, to STAR WARS: Galactic Racer. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action.".

It seems Free Play is the only place where you'll be able to access local split-screen multiplayer in Star Wars Galactic Racer, but that's no surprise considering how solo-focused the main campaign is. They'd literally have to rewrite massive portions of the campaign if they were going to implement split-screen into it.

Anyway, this is just an amazing bonus on top of an already amazing game, and I encourage you to check it out if you enjoy a title like Burnout 3: Takedown - it's fast-paced and frantic, has the same kind of takedown system that you'll remember from that game, and the roguelite campaign is really well designed (online is great fun as well).

If you've played it, let us know what you think of the game in the poll down below!

Recent findings suggest that excited for local multiplayer in Star Wars Galactic Racer? Tell us in the comments section.

It has been revealed that what if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? Industry observers note that it's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

It has been revealed that A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

In a recent development, alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

In a recent development, when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

It has been revealed that based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical firm. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

In a recent development, A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a fresh, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

In a recent development, coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate promptly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

In a recent development, there's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very rapidly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she stated, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

This N7 Day was the first without developer BioWare around, but fans of the Mass Effect series didn't let 7th November go by quietly. The community managed to get several notable Mass Effect actors to lend their voice to the increasingly loud 'SaveMassEffect' movement.

In the weeks since BioWare's shock closure and Mass Effect Universe's cancellation, the community-organised We Are Mass Effect group have put up billboards in Times Square, a mobile billboard outside BioWare Edmonton's former office and much more while directing attention to an online petition.

Recent findings suggest that today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very notable message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect. https://t.co/FOp0qp4wBI.

Sources indicate that and for the series' annual celebration, the group managed to get a sizable portion of the Mass Effect cast to join in. Commander Shepard actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer, original trilogy composer Sam Hulick, Garrus' Brandon Keener, Jack's Courtnay Taylor, Tali'Zorah's Ash Sroka, Thane's Keythe Farley and many more all highlighted up in a two-minute video to help potentially salvage the series - sometimes in character.

Sources indicate that "When we heard about the formal closing of Boware, I felt weirdly hopeful," Hale said in a separate interview with IGN. "I can't explain it. I just got so weirdly hopeful. My first thought, of course, was for the devs and all the people. And then I just closed my eyes and crossed my fingers and I said, 'I feel something's possible. You know, something's really possible.'".

The other half of Commander Shepard, Mark Meer, noted that "this didn't all just happen in the last 10 days." Near yearly layoffs at EA had slowly trimmed multiple BioWare teams down, sometimes even affecting studio veterans who had been at the company for decades.

Recent findings suggest that "A lot of senior writers within the last year or two were let go. People who had been there from the very beginning. Again, people who had built that firm from the ground up, who built the bones of it, who made those games that had captured people so much right back from the 1990s," Meer said.
